note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; code is spelled the way it is said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: The shell runs one job by hand.
A C-I pipeline runs the same commands on every change... and stops at the first failure.
This refresher covers the loop around it: review, tests, C-I, version numbers, and pinned dependencies.
All familiar? Swipe on.
A review has an order... and the order is a priority.
Take the broad view first. Then the design of the main part. If something big is wrong, say so right away.
Then functionality, complexity, tests, and naming.
Style comes last. It's a nit the author may skip.
Approve when the change clearly improves the code... not when it's perfect.
Keep pull requests small. About a hundred lines is reasonable. A thousand is usually too large.
And answer within one business day.
Now a unit test. It's the bisect oracle from the Git refresher, grown up.
One test, parametrized: one case for every input, and each passes or fails on its own.
A fixture hands each test a fresh temporary file.
But does it fail when the code is broken?
Run it on commit seven hundred thirty-one... and four tests fail.
Two still pass, because lowercasing fixes the capital P. Only the padded spellings get caught.
The run exits with one... and the gate closes.
A C-I job is the shell's pipeline of processes, laid end to end.
Each step is a new shell, and its exit status is its verdict.
The first non-zero status fails the job... and every step after it is skipped.
On the left, the fix goes green.
On the right, the regression stops at the tests. The diff step never runs.
Make the job a required check, and a red run blocks the merge.
Here's the shell refresher's trap, on a C-I runner.
This step sets no shell. Its first command can't open the file, and fails. The other two succeed.
So... does the step pass, or fail?
answer: It passes. With no shell set, GitHub runs bash with the stop-on-error option, but without pipe-fail.
So the pipeline's status is the last command's... zero. The failure is hidden.
Ask for bash explicitly, and pipe-fail switches on. Now the step fails, as it should.

lines: A flaky test passes and fails on the same code.
Here, the test compared the order of a set. And Python shuffles its string hashes, differently in every process.
Run it twenty times, and half the runs fail.
Re-running until it's green hides the problem. And a gate nobody trusts hides real failures, too.
Fix the cause. Here... sort first.
A version number is a promise.
The library is at version one point five. A fix bumps the last number. A compatible addition bumps the middle one.
Now the next release renames an output column. Which version is it?
answer: Version two. Every reader of the old column breaks, so that's an incompatible change.
The first number goes up, and the other two reset to zero.
And a released version never changes... so you can't just rebuild one point five.

lines: Works on my machine.
The requirements file says the library, version one point four or later.
Your laptop installed one point five last week, and the tests pass. Today, version two is published, with the renamed column.
What does a fresh C-I run get?
answer: It gets version two... and the app fails with a missing-key error.
Or later admits every later version, and pip takes the newest one that matches.
A library should say what it supports: below the next major version. An application should pin exactly.

lines: A lock file freezes the tree.
An application pins every package, dependencies included, with an exact version and a hash of the exact file.
With hash checking on, pip installs those bytes... or nothing.
Say someone republishes the same version with different contents. The hash doesn't match, and pip refuses.
A lock guarantees the same install, wherever it fits. It doesn't promise that it's correct.
So... eight things to keep.
Review design first, in small changes. Tests have to fail on the bug.
C-I stops at the first non-zero exit, and explicit bash adds pipe-fail. Flaky tests need their state fixed.
Versions: fix, add, or break. Libraries allow a range. Applications pin, with a lock.
Next up... the last of the five refreshers: the notation for how costs grow.
